planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; give newly set divisions regular water the first season while roots establish.

directions: As the species that lent the genus its common description, Aspidistra typica carries unusually broad, plain glossy dark-green leaves on upright petioles, forming a bold, architectural clump that reads more coarse-textured than the common cast iron plant. Small purplish, bell-shaped flowers are produced singly at ground level in late winter, hidden beneath the foliage and fallen leaf litter where they are pollinated by soil-dwelling insects rather than typical pollinators. The rhizome has a history of use in traditional Chinese herbal preparations, though the plant is grown ornamentally today strictly for its handsome, undemanding foliage. Once established it shrugs off deep dry shade, root competition from trees, and long stretches of neglect, needing only an occasional thinning of old leaves to stay tidy.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade; this mountain Sichuan species tolerates cooler winters than many of its southern Chinese relatives.

directions: This is the wild, unselected species from the forests of Sichuan Province that has served as the parent stock for a number of the spotted and striped named cultivars now popular with collectors, and in its plain form it carries lance-shaped, deep green leaves without the showy patterning of its garden offspring. Clumps spread slowly outward by thick underground rhizomes, forming a dense low groundcover over several seasons in consistently shaded beds. Inconspicuous purple-and-cream flowers appear at soil level in late winter, typically hidden under the foliage and leaf litter. Coming from relatively cool mountain forests, the species tolerates colder winter minimums than many of the more tropical Aspidistra species and needs little beyond an annual cleanup of tattered leaves.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; grow as a container or protected patio plant north of zone 8.

directions: Native to the subtropical forest floor of southern China and Taiwan, this species takes its name from its slender leaf blades, which draw out to a long, finely tapered point rather than the more rounded tip typical of the common cast iron plant; some taxonomists treat it as a variety of Aspidistra elatior rather than a fully distinct species. Clumps stay compact and tidy compared to larger-growing Aspidistra species, making it a good choice for small shaded containers or tight woodland-garden niches. It carries the same tolerance for deep shade, root competition, and dry soil once settled in, but is noticeably more cold-tender than typical Aspidistra elatior and should be mulched heavily or moved under cover where winter lows regularly dip below the mid-teens.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; best grown as a container or houseplant north of zone 8.

directions: A genuinely dwarf species native to northeastern Guangxi, China, Aspidistra retusa takes its name from the notched, retuse tip of each leaf, a distinctive detail that separates it at a glance from the many pointed-leaf cast iron plants. Leaves carry irregular silvery mottling and stay low and clump-forming, rarely reaching more than knee height, which makes it better suited to a shaded container, trough, or terrarium-scale planting than a broad groundcover role. Like its larger relatives it tolerates heavy shade and infrequent watering once rooted in, but its more tropical origin leaves it considerably less cold-hardy than Aspidistra elatior, so gardeners outside the warmest zones typically grow it in pots that can be sheltered during hard freezes. Its tiny, ground-level flowers are rarely noticed and the plant is grown entirely for its foliage.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; grow in a container where winters dip below zone 8.

directions: True to its name, this species native to southern China and Hong Kong carries unusually narrow, almost grass-like strap leaves, a sharply different texture from the broad paddle-shaped foliage typical of the genus and one that makes it a favorite textural accent among Aspidistra collectors, who also grow it under the trade name Chinese Ribbon Plant. Thin, wiry rhizomes slowly knit established plantings into a fine, arching clump in constantly shaded ground, with the same hidden, ground-level flowers common to the genus appearing in late winter. It shares the family's tolerance for dry, root-filled shade once established, but being native to warmer parts of southern China, it is markedly less cold-tolerant than common cast iron plant and performs best as a protected patio or container specimen outside the warmest zones.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; protect in a container or sheltered bed north of zone 8.

directions: Described from Sichuan Province, China, this species is grown by Aspidistra collectors for its irregular silvery-gray mottling scattered across otherwise deep green leaves, a pattern distinct from the more regular spotting seen on many Guangxi selections. It forms a modest, slow-spreading clump of moderate height, suited to a shaded border edge or specimen pot rather than large-scale groundcover duty. Culture follows the rest of the genus: deep, dry shade and root competition from nearby trees cause it no trouble once it is established, and fertilizer needs are minimal. Its subtropical origin makes it more cold-sensitive than common cast iron plant, so in zone 7 and cooler it is best kept as a container plant that can be moved under cover for winter.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
